fix regression in some multiline comment parsing

We don't have a mask for endComment matching, and the single line
comment mask got dropped in when I was find/replacing stuff. Using 0xFF
as a mask will match anything, which is a quick fix.

bound goroutine counts

scc was starting to be capable of launching goroutines at a rate which
can lead to launching too many OS threads:

* linux-4.19-rc1 on a 16 core c5.4xlarge:
runtime: failed to create new OS thread (have 4090 already; errno=11)
runtime: may need to increase max user processes (ulimit -u)
fatal error: newosproc

this change bounds the number of goroutine workers to avoid this, while
still creating enough to saturate the CPU. This includes a marginal
improvement in performance, and appears to make the runtime much more
consistent:

* linux-4.19-rc1 on a 4 core c5.xlarge:
before: Time (mean ± σ):      4.680 s ±  0.727 s    [User: 17.920 s, System: 0.632 s]
after:  Time (mean ± σ):      4.532 s ±  0.005 s    [User: 17.340 s, System: 0.705 s]

fix: resolve HEAD in git worktrees (#765) (#766)

Every history report rendered "no commits" when run inside a linked git
worktree, against a repo with full history.

scc opened repositories with PlainOpenWithOptions{DetectDotGit: true} in
three places. DetectDotGit correctly follows the `gitdir:` pointer in the
.git *file* a worktree has in place of a .git directory, which lands
go-git in .git/worktrees/<name>. That directory holds the worktree's own
HEAD but an empty refs/ — the real refs live in the main repository,
reachable only through the `commondir` file beside that HEAD. go-git only
reads commondir when EnableDotGitCommonDir is set, which it was not.

So a worktree opened successfully and then resolved nothing: HEAD came
back as ErrReferenceNotFound, runHistory took that for a freshly
initialised repo, and the empty window rendered as "no commits". Both
detectGit and --coupling-for's pre-walk target check were affected too;
the latter silently accepted paths absent from HEAD.

Collapse the three copies of the open options into one openRepository
helper with both options set, so they cannot drift apart again. Both are
inert outside a worktree: an ordinary checkout has no commondir file.

An unborn HEAD and an unresolvable HEAD are the same error with no signal
to tell them apart, so runHistory no longer swallows it silently — it
warns before treating the repo as empty. Verbose-gated like every other
warning, so this is a diagnostic aid rather than an alarm, but --verbose
now says something where it previously said nothing.

Tests fabricate the worktree layout on disk rather than shelling out to
`git worktree add`, needing no git binary, matching how the shallow-clone
fixture is built.

perf: count the kernel in half the time, and count it correctly (#771)

Two strands of work on the same branch: a conformance pass that fixed what scc
was counting, and a performance pass that halved what it cost.

Over the Linux kernel, 85,899 files and 1.5GB, against the previous release:

  default   508.6ms -> 231.0ms
  -c        445.7ms -> 186.4ms
  -c --exp-per-language-counters      156.8ms
  the walk alone                       39.9ms

CONFORMANCE

Measured against LineJudge, which scored scc 56/83 at the start of this branch
and 74/83 now. Two of the fixes are not edge cases.

38 languages had no working double quoted string. The delimiter was written
"\\\"" in languages.json, a literal backslash in front of a quote, from
escaping twice into JSON, and had been since 2018. Shell, Ruby, TOML, Zig,
Julia, Nim, Dockerfile, Zsh and thirty more. A single line string hid it,
because that line counts as code either way; it only showed on a multi line
string whose continuation opened with a comment token.

The C family now splices lines joined by a backslash. A line comment carries
onto the next line, and a string does not, which is the rule that mattered:
*str == '"' in drivers/acpi/osl.c opened a string that nothing closed, and
every one of the 381 lines below it counted as code to the end of the file.

The rest: block comments nest in ten more languages, CMake bracket comments and
bracket arguments at every level, Groovy's four string forms, SQL where a
backslash does not escape a quote, PowerShell's backtick, an apostrophe in
markup, a line comment spelled as a word ending where the word does, and the
closer of a C++ raw string read out of the file.

PERFORMANCE

Counters written by hand for C, C Header and Java, behind
--exp-per-language-counters, where the generic loop is driven by a trie built
from the language table. A table and a switch answer what the trie was asked at
every byte. The anchor for each complexity check is its rarest byte rather than
its first, read backwards, which drops e, i and s from the stop set: the scan
stops on 10.5% of bytes where it stopped on 21.5%.

The generic loop got the same idea in weaker form. It asked ProcessMask, an OR
of the first byte of every token, which for most languages is 0x7f, so nearly
every byte cleared it and paid for a trie walk that failed at its first step. A
256 entry table answers exactly instead.

The pipeline stopped starving itself. Building file jobs ran on one goroutine
between a queue that was always full and one that was always empty, which is
the definition of a bottleneck: 97,730 futex calls over the kernel, 1.14 per
file, down to 5,571 on a pool. Files now arrive from the walker a directory at
a time rather than one at a time, the walking goroutines having spent 44% of
their life blocked in that send.

Files are read with the system calls rather than through os.Open, which
registered every descriptor with the netpoller for an epoll_ctl that always
failed. The read buffer grows rather than being thrown away whenever a large
file went past it, which had every worker re-climbing the doubling ladder and
zeroing each rung.

Deciding whether a .h is C, C++ or Objective C ran a scan of the file head per
literal, 37 of them for each of 26,167 headers. A plan answers them in a handful
of passes, screening on the rarest byte of each literal rather than its first.

Where the output only wants per language totals the counting workers fold their
own and merge once, rather than sending every file to a single goroutine.

Also picks up gocodewalker: a directory walk that uses more than one core, the
gitignore matcher off the hot path, the walk root resolved once rather than
every path against every ignore file, and the common gitignore patterns
answered without fnmatch.

Output is byte identical to the previous release throughout, verified over the
Linux kernel, llama.cpp, ComfyUI, a Java corpus and scc itself, per file and
per language, across the output formats and the flags that reach this code.
go test ./... and go test -race pass.

Review found six more, all fixed here.

A block comment that nothing closes, on a line that never ends, cost time in
the square of its length under the per language counters: the comment state
reported the index it started from rather than the last byte it looked at, so
the loop above stepped on one byte and handed the whole tail back. 250KB took
eleven seconds and a megabyte took three minutes. Now the same as every other
state, and a megabyte is not measurable.

A string whose opener is also most of its closer never closed when it was
empty. The cursor was left past the opening token where every other path leaves
it on the last byte of it, so the byte the caller looked at next was the one
after the closer: '' in SQL, [[]] in Lua, `` in Go and '''''' in Python each
swallowed every line under them. That is the same shape as the unterminated
string this branch already fixed for C.

A C++ raw string naming a delimiter of the full sixteen bytes was not
recognised, the scan stopping one byte before the bracket that ends it, and the
plain quote it fell back to ran to the end of the file.

--file-list-job-workers 0 and --file-process-job-workers 0 started no
goroutines, so nothing drained the queue, the stage below saw it closed, and
the run reported a tree of no files and exited successfully. Both take a floor
of one worker.

The descriptor is opened O_CLOEXEC, which os.Open set and the direct system
call did not, so a file being counted cannot leak into a child process.

The counters read the byte in front of a quote to decide whether it is escaped,
which cannot happen at the first byte given the states start blank, but the
reads are guarded rather than resting on it.

Counts are unchanged on the kernel, llama.cpp and wise. They change on scc's
own tree, where detector_test.go holds an empty Go raw string that was
swallowing the ten lines under it: nine blank and one comment, which is exactly
what moves.

A name is trimmed to the column width by grapheme cluster rather than by rune,
because that is what StringWidth answers and the two disagree: a family emoji is
four runes joined by zero width joiners and two cells wide, where the runes add
up to eight. Summing runes cut a name that already fitted, and cut it through
the middle of the cluster, leaving a dangling joiner. It costs about 3% of a
--by-file run and is still nothing beside the one at a time version it replaced.

The read loop was going to stop at the size the stat gave rather than reading
until it was told zero, which saved half the read calls, 179,668 down to 90,247
over the kernel, for about five milliseconds of system time in a five second
run. A short read does not establish the end of a file, so that made the count
depend on whether the filesystem underneath chops reads up. Not worth a tenth of
a percent, and the loop reads to the end again.

Two more from review, both a language reading a comment token the way the
language actually reads it.

Batch and ASP read their keywords in any case, so REM, rem and rEm all open a
comment, where only the first was recognised. A language says so with
caseinsensitive, and the spellings are expanded when it is compiled rather than
the match being folded, which keeps case out of the counting loop: it walks a
trie of bytes and still knows nothing about letters. The word boundary is
unaffected, so REMOVE is a command whatever the case of it. A token of more
letters than is sensible is left as written rather than becoming a thousand
entries.

Forth writes a line comment as a backslash, which is a word like any other, so
it opens a comment only where it stands alone: "\ x" is a comment and "\x" is
not. The boundary a token gets for free is worked out from the token ending in
a letter, which a backslash does not, so the language declares it with
commentisword.
